SECURITY DEPOSIT ITEMIZATION / MOVE-OUT STATEMENT
Prepared for Pat Morgan · Jordan Lee

DEPOSIT DETAILS
SECURITY DEPOSIT ITEMIZATION / MOVE-OUT STATEMENT. Landlord: Pat Morgan. Tenant: Jordan Lee. Property: 123 Main St., Apt. 4, Sacramento, CA 95814. Security deposit received: $2,200, received on or about September 1, 2024. Tenant vacated the property on August 31, 2026. This statement is dated September 15, 2026 and sets out the disposition of the security deposit described above.

THE STATUTORY CAP ON THE DEPOSIT AMOUNT
Under California statute, a landlord generally may not demand or receive a security deposit, however denominated, in excess of one month's rent, in addition to the first month's rent paid on or before initial occupancy. A narrower exception permits a higher cap of two months' rent, but only for a landlord who is a natural person (or an LLC whose members are all natural persons) and who owns no more than two residential rental properties totaling no more than four dwelling units offered for rent combined — and even that higher cap does not apply if the prospective tenant is a service member, in which case the one-month cap still controls. This general one-month cap took effect for security collected or demanded on or after July 1, 2024; it does not apply to security collected or demanded before that date. Separately, and not subject to the cap described above, a landlord may require an advance rent payment of not less than six months' rent if the lease term is six months or longer.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "a landlord shall not demand or receive security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of an amount equal to one month's rent, in addition to any rent for the first month paid on or before initial occupancy."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(c)(1), California Civil Code, general one-month security deposit cap (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.5.)
  "a landlord shall not demand or receive security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of an amount equal to two months' rent, in addition to any rent for the first month paid on or before initial occupancy if the landlord meets both of the following requirements: (i) The landlord is a natural person or a limited liability company in which all members are natural persons. (ii) The landlord owns no more than two residential rental properties that collectively include no more than four dwelling units offered for rent."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(c)(5)(A), California Civil Code, higher cap for a small individual landlord (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.5.)
  "Subparagraph (A) shall not apply if the prospective tenant is a service member."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(c)(5)(B), California Civil Code, the small-landlord cap doesn't apply to a service-member tenant (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.5.)
  "This subdivision shall not apply to a security collected or demanded by the landlord before July 1, 2024."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(c)(6), California Civil Code, effective date of the general cap (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.5.)
  "This subdivision does not prohibit an advance payment of not less than six months' rent if the term of the lease is six months or longer."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(c)(2), California Civil Code, advance rent for a longer lease (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.5.)
  Known gap: This is California's current statutory cap, not a nationwide figure — security deposit caps vary enormously by state, from no state-level cap at all to caps expressed in different terms, and this document tracks California's statewide statute only, not the pre-July 2024 two- or three-month caps that used to apply generally and that a reader may have seen referenced in older material. This document addresses California's statewide statute only; it does not cover any city or county's local rent-control or security-deposit ordinance that might impose its own, different rule. All citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (Civil Code § 1950.5) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

PERMITTED USES OF THE DEPOSIT — AND THE ORDINARY WEAR-AND-TEAR CARVE-OUT
Under California statute, a security deposit may be used only for the following purposes, subject to the further limits described below: (1) compensating the landlord for a tenant's default in the payment of rent; (2) repairing damage to the premises caused by the tenant or the tenant's guest or licensee, exclusive of ordinary wear and tear; (3) cleaning the premises at the end of the tenancy, to the extent necessary to return the unit to the same level of cleanliness it was in at the start of the tenancy; and (4) remedying a future default by the tenant in an obligation to restore, replace, or return personal property or appurtenances, exclusive of ordinary wear and tear, but only if the rental agreement authorizes the deposit to be applied to that purpose. Beyond this list, a landlord may claim from the deposit only amounts that are reasonably necessary for those purposes, and may not assert a claim against the deposit for damage or a defective condition that predates the tenancy, for ordinary wear and tear or its effects (whether the wear and tear predates or occurs during the tenancy), or for the cumulative effect of ordinary wear and tear across one or more tenancies.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "(1) The compensation of a landlord for a tenant's default in the payment of rent. (2) The repair of damages to the premises, exclusive of ordinary wear and tear, caused by the tenant or by a guest or licensee of the tenant. (3) The cleaning of the premises upon termination of the tenancy necessary to return the unit to the same level of cleanliness it was in at the inception of the tenancy."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(b), California Civil Code, the first three permitted uses of a security deposit (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.5.)
  "(4) To remedy future defaults by the tenant in any obligation under the rental agreement to restore, replace, or return personal property or appurtenances, exclusive of ordinary wear and tear, if the security deposit is authorized to be applied thereto by the rental agreement."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(b)(4), California Civil Code, the fourth permitted use — future personal-property defaults (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.5.)
  "the landlord may claim of the security only those amounts as are reasonably necessary for the purposes specified in subdivision (b)."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(e)(1), California Civil Code, the "reasonably necessary" limit on a claim (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.5.)
  "The landlord shall not assert a claim against the tenant or the security for damages to the premises or any defective conditions that preexisted the tenancy, for ordinary wear and tear or the effects thereof, whether the wear and tear preexisted the tenancy or occurred during the tenancy, or for the cumulative effects of ordinary wear and tear occurring during any one or more tenancies."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(e)(2)(A), California Civil Code, the affirmative bar on a wear-and-tear or pre-existing-condition claim (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.5.)
  Known gap: The "ordinary wear and tear" exclusion is a real, litigated line rather than a formality — the statute repeats it separately for damage repair, for the fourth (personal-property) use, and again as an affirmative bar on any claim for wear and tear regardless of when it occurred, but the statute itself does not define what counts as "ordinary" wear and tear as opposed to tenant-caused damage; that line is drawn case by case rather than by a statutory checklist. This is one state's exhaustive statutory list — other states permit different, and sometimes broader or narrower, categories of deductions, and this document does not track any state's law but California's, and only the statewide rule, not any city or county ordinance that might narrow it further. All citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (Civil Code § 1950.5) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

TENANT'S RIGHT TO A PRE-MOVE-OUT INSPECTION
Before Tenant moves out, Landlord must notify Tenant in writing of Tenant's option to request an initial (pre-move-out) inspection and the right to be present for it. If Tenant requests one, Landlord must inspect no earlier than two weeks before the move-out date and give Tenant at least 48 hours' written notice of the inspection date and time. The point of this inspection is to let Tenant fix any identified problems before move-out, to avoid a deduction from the deposit for them.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-30]
  "Within a reasonable time after notification of either party’s intention to terminate the tenancy, or before the end of the lease term, the landlord shall notify the tenant in writing of the tenant’s option to request an initial inspection and of the tenant’s right to be present at the inspection. At a reasonable time, but no earlier than two weeks before the termination or the end of lease date, the landlord, or an agent of the landlord, shall, upon the request of the tenant, make an initial inspection of the premises prior to any final inspection the landlord makes after the tenant has vacated the premises. The purpose of the initial inspection shall be to allow the tenant an opportunity to remedy identified deficiencies, in a manner consistent with the rights and obligations of the parties under the rental agreement, in order to avoid deductions from the security."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(f)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the pre-move-out inspection right (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.5.)
  "The landlord shall give at least 48 hours’ prior written notice of the date and time of the inspection if either a mutual time is agreed upon, or if a mutually agreed time cannot be scheduled but the tenant still wishes an inspection."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(f)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, 48-hour inspection notice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.5.)
  "if an initial inspection is conducted pursuant to this subdivision and, at the time of inspection, the premises do not contain tenant possessions that prevent the landlord from identifying repairs or cleanings due to the presence of those possessions, the landlord shall not use the security for deductions for repairs or cleanings that are not identified in the itemized statement described in paragraph (2)."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(f)(4) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, effect of not identifying an issue at the inspection (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.5.)
  "The requirements of this subdivision do not apply when the tenancy is terminated pursuant to subdivision (2), (3), or (4) of Section 1161 of the Code of Civil Procedure."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(f)(7) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, this right doesn't apply to a for-cause unlawful detainer (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.5.)
  Known gap: If Tenant requests this inspection and the unit isn't full of Tenant's belongings in a way that would hide problems from view, Landlord generally can't later deduct from the deposit for a repair or cleaning issue that wasn't identified at that inspection. This is a real, concrete consequence of the inspection right, not just a formality — and it's easy to miss because the inspection itself is optional (Tenant has to request it; if Tenant doesn't, this whole process — and its protection — doesn't apply). This entire inspection right doesn't apply at all if the tenancy is ending through an unlawful detainer based on nonpayment of rent, a lease breach, or waste/nuisance — those specific for-cause terminations void the right described in this clause. This is one state's statute; not every state gives tenants this specific right. All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1950.5) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

THE 21-DAY ITEMIZATION AND REFUND DEADLINE
Under California statute, no later than 21 calendar days after the tenant has vacated the premises, the landlord must furnish the tenant a copy of an itemized statement indicating the basis for, and the amount of, any security received and its disposition, and must return any remaining portion of the deposit to the tenant. Along with that itemized statement, the landlord must also include copies of documents showing the charges deducted — bills, invoices, or receipts for repair or cleaning work performed by someone other than the landlord, or a description of the work and the time and hourly rate charged if the landlord or the landlord's employee performed it. If a repair cannot reasonably be completed within the 21-day period, or if supporting documents from a person or entity providing services, materials, or supplies are not yet in the landlord's possession within that period, the landlord may instead deduct a good-faith estimate of the charges and provide that estimate with the itemized statement, then complete the documentation requirements within 14 calendar days after the repair is finished or the documentation is received. A landlord need not provide supporting documents at all — for either the initial statement or the later completion — if the total deductions for repairs and cleaning combined do not exceed $125, or if the tenant has separately signed a written waiver of that documentation right.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "No later than 21 calendar days after the tenant has vacated the premises, but not earlier than the time that either the landlord or the tenant provides a notice to terminate the tenancy under Section 1946 or 1946.1, Section 1161 of the Code of Civil Procedure, or not earlier than 60 calendar days prior to the expiration of a fixed-term lease, the landlord shall furnish the tenant, a copy of an itemized statement indicating the basis for, and the amount of, any security received and the disposition of the security, and shall return any remaining portion of the security to the tenant..."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(h)(1), California Civil Code, the 21-day itemization and refund deadline (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.5.)
  "If a repair to be done by the landlord or the landlord's employee cannot reasonably be completed within 21 calendar days after the tenant has vacated the premises, or if the documents from a person or entity providing services, materials, or supplies are not in the landlord's possession within 21 calendar days after the tenant has vacated the premises, the landlord may deduct the amount of a good faith estimate of the charges that will be incurred and provide that estimate with the itemized statement. ...Within 14 calendar days of completing the repair or receiving the documentation, the landlord shall complete the requirements in paragraphs (1) and (2) in the manner specified."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(h)(3), California Civil Code, the good-faith-estimate alternative when work isn't done in 21 days (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.5.)
  "The landlord need not comply with paragraph (2) or (3) if either of the following applies: (A) The deductions for repairs and cleaning together do not exceed one hundred twenty-five dollars ($125)."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(h)(4)(A), California Civil Code, the $125 documentation threshold (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.5.)
  "The landlord shall not be entitled to claim any amount of the security if the landlord, in bad faith, fails to comply with this subdivision."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(h)(7), California Civil Code, forfeiture for bad-faith noncompliance with this subdivision (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.5.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statutory deadline and documentation threshold, not a nationwide figure — the length of the return/itemization period, and whether receipts are required at all, vary considerably by state. This document addresses California's statewide statute only, not any city or county ordinance that might impose additional or different move-out documentation requirements. The 21-day period does not start running before the landlord or tenant gives notice to terminate the tenancy (or, for a fixed-term lease, no earlier than 60 calendar days before the lease's expiration) — a timing nuance distinct from the 21-day outer deadline itself and easy to overlook. A landlord who, in bad faith, fails to comply with this itemization and documentation subdivision is not entitled to claim any amount of the security at all — a separate and more severe consequence than the general bad-faith penalty described elsewhere in this document. All citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (Civil Code § 1950.5) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

ITEMIZED DEDUCTIONS SCHEDULE
ITEMIZED DEDUCTIONS. The following amounts are deducted from the security deposit of $2,200 described above, each identified by category, description, and amount:

1. Unpaid rent: $0 — description: N/A
2. Repair of damage beyond ordinary wear and tear: $250 — description: Repair of hole in living room wall
3. Cleaning necessary to return the unit to its move-in level of cleanliness: $100 — description: Carpet cleaning
4. Remedying a future default in returning or restoring personal property (only if authorized by the rental agreement): $0 — description: N/A

Total deductions: $350. Remaining deposit refunded to Jordan Lee: $1,850.

Supporting documentation. Copies of bills, invoices, or receipts for the deductions listed above (or, where work was not complete, a good-faith estimate) are attached to this statement as Exhibit A, except for any deduction category exempted from that documentation requirement by its dollar amount or by a signed waiver.

BAD-FAITH RETENTION: THE PENALTY FOR IMPROPERLY WITHHOLDING A DEPOSIT
Under California statute, if a landlord (or the landlord's successor in interest) claims or retains a security deposit in bad faith, in violation of the security-deposit statute, the landlord may be liable for statutory damages of up to twice the amount of the deposit, in addition to actual damages — meaning the up-to-double penalty is added on top of whatever actual damages the tenant proves, not a cap that replaces or absorbs them. A court may award this bad-faith penalty whenever the facts warrant it, even if the tenant did not specifically request that relief. In any action under this statute, the landlord bears the burden of proving the reasonableness of amounts claimed against the deposit, or the landlord's authority to demand additional security. An action to recover a wrongfully retained deposit — including both actual and statutory damages — may be brought in small claims court if the total claimed falls within that court's jurisdictional dollar limit.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "The bad faith claim or retention by a landlord or the landlord's successors in interest of the security or any portion thereof in violation of this section, or the bad faith demand of replacement of security in violation of subdivision (k), may subject the landlord or the landlord's successors in interest to statutory damages of up to twice the amount of the security, in addition to actual damages. The court may award damages for bad faith whenever the facts warrant that award, regardless of whether the injured party has specifically requested relief. In an action under this section, the landlord or the landlord's successors in interest shall have the burden of proof as to the reasonableness of the amounts claimed or the authority pursuant to this section to demand additional security deposits."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(m), California Civil Code, the bad-faith retention penalty (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.5.)
  "The landlord shall not be entitled to claim any amount of the security if the landlord, in bad faith, fails to comply with this subdivision."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(h)(7) [forfeiture], California Civil Code, forfeiture of the entire deposit for bad-faith itemization noncompliance (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.5.)
  "An action under this section may be maintained in small claims court if the damages claimed, whether actual, statutory, or both, are within the jurisdictional amount allowed by Section 116.220 or 116.221 of the Code of Civil Procedure."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(o), California Civil Code, small claims court jurisdiction over these damages (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.5.)
  Known gap: "Bad faith" is not defined by a fixed statutory checklist here; it is a standard applied to the facts of each case, and a landlord's good-faith interpretation of what may be deducted, or a good-faith accounting error, is not automatically bad faith. This is one state's statutory remedy; the amount, structure, and even the existence of a bad-faith deposit-retention penalty vary by state, and this document addresses California's statewide statute only, not any city or county ordinance. All citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (Civil Code § 1950.5) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

INTEREST ON THE DEPOSIT: NOT REQUIRED BY THIS STATUTE
California's security-deposit statute — the same statute that sets the deposit cap, the permitted uses, the 21-day return deadline, and the bad-faith penalty described elsewhere in this document — contains no provision requiring a landlord to pay interest on a tenant's security deposit while it is held. Its only references to the word "interest" anywhere in the statute concern a landlord's "interest in the premises" (ownership) and a landlord's "successor in interest" on a sale or transfer of the property — an unrelated legal use of the same word, not a security-deposit interest-payment obligation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "As used in this section, "security" means any payment, fee, deposit, or charge, including, but not limited to, any payment, fee, deposit, or charge, except as provided in Section 1950.6, that is imposed at the beginning of the tenancy to be used to reimburse the landlord for costs associated with processing a new tenant or that is imposed as an advance payment of rent, used or to be used for any purpose, including, but not limited to, any of the following: (1) The compensation of a landlord for a tenant's default in the payment of rent. (2) The repair of damages to the premises, exclusive of ordinary wear and tear, caused by the tenant or by a guest or licensee of the tenant. (3) The cleaning of the premises upon termination of the tenancy necessary to return the unit to the same level of cleanliness it was in at the inception of the tenancy. (4) To remedy future defaults by the tenant in any obligation under the rental agreement to restore, replace, or return personal property or appurtenances, exclusive of ordinary wear and tear, if the security deposit is authorized to be applied thereto by the rental agreement."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(b), California Civil Code, the full definitional/permitted-use provision, containing no interest obligation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.5.)
  "(Amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 340, Sec. 1. (AB 414) Effective January 1, 2026.)"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5 [amendment history], California Civil Code, confirming the currently operative, fully reviewed version of the section (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1950.5.)
  Known gap: This is a negative finding based on direct review of the current, complete text of California Civil Code section 1950.5 (the statute governing residential security deposits statewide) — not a claim that no California jurisdiction anywhere requires deposit interest. A number of California cities and counties with local rent-control or tenant-protection ordinances (San Francisco and Berkeley are commonly cited examples) separately require a landlord to pay tenants interest on a held security deposit, sometimes annually, under those local ordinances — but that obligation comes from municipal or county law, not from the statewide Civil Code section on which this document is based, and this document does not track any city's or county's local ordinance. Deposit-interest requirements also vary by state at the state level; some states require it and California's statewide rule does not. This is a single statutory citation confirming the absence of an interest-payment provision in the operative, currently amended text of the section; no additional independent source was found for this.

LANDLORD SIGNATURE AND CERTIFICATION
Landlord certifies that the amounts and descriptions stated in this itemized statement are accurate to the best of Landlord's knowledge and reflect deductions for the purposes and in the amounts described in this statement.

Signed: Pat Morgan, Landlord. Date: September 15, 2026.

Delivery record. This statement, together with the refund described above and any required supporting documentation, was provided to Jordan Lee on _______________ (date) by the following method (check one): ☐ personal delivery; ☐ first-class mail, postage prepaid; ☐ email to an address provided by Tenant, by mutual written agreement; ☐ electronic delivery of the refund with the itemized statement furnished as described above.

Provided by: _______________ (name) Date: _______________

citations.quote: Within a reasonable time after notification of either party’s intention to terminate the tenancy, or before the end of the lease term, the landlord shall notify the tenant in writing of the tenant’s option to request an initial inspection and of the tenant’s right to be present at the inspection. At a reasonable time, but no earlier than two weeks before the termination or the end of lease date, the landlord, or an agent of the landlord, shall, upon the request of the tenant, make an initial inspection of the premises prior to any final inspection the landlord makes after the tenant has vacated the premises. The purpose of the initial inspection shall be to allow the tenant an opportunity to remedy identified deficiencies, in a manner consistent with the rights and obligations of the parties under the rental agreement, in order to avoid deductions from the security.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(f)(1) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, 48-hour inspection notice
citations.quote: The landlord shall give at least 48 hours’ prior written notice of the date and time of the inspection if either a mutual time is agreed upon, or if a mutually agreed time cannot be scheduled but the tenant still wishes an inspection.

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(f)(4) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, effect of not identifying an issue at the inspection
citations.quote: if an initial inspection is conducted pursuant to this subdivision and, at the time of inspection, the premises do not contain tenant possessions that prevent the landlord from identifying repairs or cleanings due to the presence of those possessions, the landlord shall not use the security for deductions for repairs or cleanings that are not identified in the itemized statement described in paragraph (2).

citations.case: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(f)(7) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: California Civil Code, this right doesn't apply to a for-cause unlawful detainer
citations.quote: The requirements of this subdivision do not apply when the tenancy is terminated pursuant to subdivision (2), (3), or (4) of Section 1161 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

expectedJSON.gap: If Tenant requests this inspection and the unit isn't full of Tenant's belongings in a way that would hide problems from view, Landlord generally can't later deduct from the deposit for a repair or cleaning issue that wasn't identified at that inspection. This is a real, concrete consequence of the inspection right, not just a formality — and it's easy to miss because the inspection itself is optional (Tenant has to request it; if Tenant doesn't, this whole process — and its protection — doesn't apply). This entire inspection right doesn't apply at all if the tenancy is ending through an unlawful detainer based on nonpayment of rent, a lease breach, or waste/nuisance — those specific for-cause terminations void the right described in this clause. This is one state's statute; not every state gives tenants this specific right. All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1950.5) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

expectedJSON.body: Under California statute, no later than 21 calendar days after the tenant has vacated the premises, the landlord must furnish the tenant a copy of an itemized statement indicating the basis for, and the amount of, any security received and its disposition, and must return any remaining portion of the deposit to the tenant. Along with that itemized statement, the landlord must also include copies of documents showing the charges deducted — bills, invoices, or receipts for repair or cleaning work performed by someone other than the landlord, or a description of the work and the time and hourly rate charged if the landlord or the landlord's employee performed it. If a repair cannot reasonably be completed within the 21-day period, or if supporting documents from a person or entity providing services, materials, or supplies are not yet in the landlord's possession within that period, the landlord may instead deduct a good-faith estimate of the charges and provide that estimate with the itemized statement, then complete the documentation requirements within 14 calendar days after the repair is finished or the documentation is received. A landlord need not provide supporting documents at all — for either the initial statement or the later completion — if the total deductions for repairs and cleaning combined do not exceed $125, or if the tenant has separately signed a written waiver of that documentation right.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, the 21-day itemization and refund deadline
citations.quote: No later than 21 calendar days after the tenant has vacated the premises, but not earlier than the time that either the landlord or the tenant provides a notice to terminate the tenancy under Section 1946 or 1946.1, Section 1161 of the Code of Civil Procedure, or not earlier than 60 calendar days prior to the expiration of a fixed-term lease, the landlord shall furnish the tenant, a copy of an itemized statement indicating the basis for, and the amount of, any security received and the disposition of the security, and shall return any remaining portion of the security to the tenant...

citations.cite: California Civil Code, the good-faith-estimate alternative when work isn't done in 21 days
citations.quote: If a repair to be done by the landlord or the landlord's employee cannot reasonably be completed within 21 calendar days after the tenant has vacated the premises, or if the documents from a person or entity providing services, materials, or supplies are not in the landlord's possession within 21 calendar days after the tenant has vacated the premises, the landlord may deduct the amount of a good faith estimate of the charges that will be incurred and provide that estimate with the itemized statement. ...Within 14 calendar days of completing the repair or receiving the documentation, the landlord shall complete the requirements in paragraphs (1) and (2) in the manner specified.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, the $125 documentation threshold
citations.quote: The landlord need not comply with paragraph (2) or (3) if either of the following applies: (A) The deductions for repairs and cleaning together do not exceed one hundred twenty-five dollars ($125).

citations.cite: California Civil Code, forfeiture for bad-faith noncompliance with this subdivision
citations.quote: The landlord shall not be entitled to claim any amount of the security if the landlord, in bad faith, fails to comply with this subdivision.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statutory deadline and documentation threshold, not a nationwide figure — the length of the return/itemization period, and whether receipts are required at all, vary considerably by state. This document addresses California's statewide statute only, not any city or county ordinance that might impose additional or different move-out documentation requirements. The 21-day period does not start running before the landlord or tenant gives notice to terminate the tenancy (or, for a fixed-term lease, no earlier than 60 calendar days before the lease's expiration) — a timing nuance distinct from the 21-day outer deadline itself and easy to overlook. A landlord who, in bad faith, fails to comply with this itemization and documentation subdivision is not entitled to claim any amount of the security at all — a separate and more severe consequence than the general bad-faith penalty described elsewhere in this document. All citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (Civil Code § 1950.5) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

expectedJSON.body:
ITEMIZED DEDUCTIONS. The following amounts are deducted from the security deposit of $2,200 described above, each identified by category, description, and amount:

1. Unpaid rent: $0 — description: N/A
2. Repair of damage beyond ordinary wear and tear: $250 — description: Repair of hole in living room wall
3. Cleaning necessary to return the unit to its move-in level of cleanliness: $100 — description: Carpet cleaning
4. Remedying a future default in returning or restoring personal property (only if authorized by the rental agreement): $0 — description: N/A

Total deductions: $350. Remaining deposit refunded to Jordan Lee: $1,850.

Supporting documentation. Copies of bills, invoices, or receipts for the deductions listed above (or, where work was not complete, a good-faith estimate) are attached to this statement as Exhibit A, except for any deduction category exempted from that documentation requirement by its dollar amount or by a signed waiver.

Under California statute, if a landlord (or the landlord's successor in interest) claims or retains a security deposit in bad faith, in violation of the security-deposit statute, the landlord may be liable for statutory damages of up to twice the amount of the deposit, in addition to actual damages — meaning the up-to-double penalty is added on top of whatever actual damages the tenant proves, not a cap that replaces or absorbs them. A court may award this bad-faith penalty whenever the facts warrant it, even if the tenant did not specifically request that relief. In any action under this statute, the landlord bears the burden of proving the reasonableness of amounts claimed against the deposit, or the landlord's authority to demand additional security. An action to recover a wrongfully retained deposit — including both actual and statutory damages — may be brought in small claims court if the total claimed falls within that court's jurisdictional dollar limit.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, the bad-faith retention penalty
citations.quote: The bad faith claim or retention by a landlord or the landlord's successors in interest of the security or any portion thereof in violation of this section, or the bad faith demand of replacement of security in violation of subdivision (k), may subject the landlord or the landlord's successors in interest to statutory damages of up to twice the amount of the security, in addition to actual damages. The court may award damages for bad faith whenever the facts warrant that award, regardless of whether the injured party has specifically requested relief. In an action under this section, the landlord or the landlord's successors in interest shall have the burden of proof as to the reasonableness of the amounts claimed or the authority pursuant to this section to demand additional security deposits.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, forfeiture of the entire deposit for bad-faith itemization noncompliance
citations.quote: The landlord shall not be entitled to claim any amount of the security if the landlord, in bad faith, fails to comply with this subdivision.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, small claims court jurisdiction over these damages
citations.quote: An action under this section may be maintained in small claims court if the damages claimed, whether actual, statutory, or both, are within the jurisdictional amount allowed by Section 116.220 or 116.221 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

expectedJSON.gap: "Bad faith" is not defined by a fixed statutory checklist here; it is a standard applied to the facts of each case, and a landlord's good-faith interpretation of what may be deducted, or a good-faith accounting error, is not automatically bad faith. This is one state's statutory remedy; the amount, structure, and even the existence of a bad-faith deposit-retention penalty vary by state, and this document addresses California's statewide statute only, not any city or county ordinance. All citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (Civil Code § 1950.5) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this.

expectedJSON.body: California's security-deposit statute — the same statute that sets the deposit cap, the permitted uses, the 21-day return deadline, and the bad-faith penalty described elsewhere in this document — contains no provision requiring a landlord to pay interest on a tenant's security deposit while it is held. Its only references to the word "interest" anywhere in the statute concern a landlord's "interest in the premises" (ownership) and a landlord's "successor in interest" on a sale or transfer of the property — an unrelated legal use of the same word, not a security-deposit interest-payment obligation.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, the full definitional/permitted-use provision, containing no interest obligation
citations.quote: As used in this section, "security" means any payment, fee, deposit, or charge, including, but not limited to, any payment, fee, deposit, or charge, except as provided in Section 1950.6, that is imposed at the beginning of the tenancy to be used to reimburse the landlord for costs associated with processing a new tenant or that is imposed as an advance payment of rent, used or to be used for any purpose, including, but not limited to, any of the following: (1) The compensation of a landlord for a tenant's default in the payment of rent. (2) The repair of damages to the premises, exclusive of ordinary wear and tear, caused by the tenant or by a guest or licensee of the tenant. (3) The cleaning of the premises upon termination of the tenancy necessary to return the unit to the same level of cleanliness it was in at the inception of the tenancy. (4) To remedy future defaults by the tenant in any obligation under the rental agreement to restore, replace, or return personal property or appurtenances, exclusive of ordinary wear and tear, if the security deposit is authorized to be applied thereto by the rental agreement.

citations.cite: California Civil Code, confirming the currently operative, fully reviewed version of the section
citations.quote: (Amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 340, Sec. 1. (AB 414) Effective January 1, 2026.)

expectedJSON.gap: This is a negative finding based on direct review of the current, complete text of California Civil Code section 1950.5 (the statute governing residential security deposits statewide) — not a claim that no California jurisdiction anywhere requires deposit interest. A number of California cities and counties with local rent-control or tenant-protection ordinances (San Francisco and Berkeley are commonly cited examples) separately require a landlord to pay tenants interest on a held security deposit, sometimes annually, under those local ordinances — but that obligation comes from municipal or county law, not from the statewide Civil Code section on which this document is based, and this document does not track any city's or county's local ordinance. Deposit-interest requirements also vary by state at the state level; some states require it and California's statewide rule does not. This is a single statutory citation confirming the absence of an interest-payment provision in the operative, currently amended text of the section; no additional independent source was found for this.
